NEW PATIENT

26 y/o woman here to set up primary care. No active complaints. Coming from another office; records requested 8/30, not here yet.

PMH: none she knows of. Nearsighted, glasses since she was a kid; hasn't had an eye exam in a little while.
PSH: none.
Meds: none. Occasional acetaminophen for headache, rarely.
Allergies: none to medications.

Family: mother treated for major depression. Father very nearsighted, had a retinal detachment repaired years ago. She thinks someone on one side had a stroke but can't say who. An uncle on mom's side has schizophrenia. Sister healthy. Mom's family is Ashkenazi Jewish.

Social: works full time as an administrative assistant at an office in town. Married. She and her husband live with her older sister, the house is the sister's. Never smoked, doesn't drink, no drug use. Medicaid.

ROS: negative across the board on a written questionnaire, reviewed with her.

Exam: vitals in flowsheet, all normal. Slim, well appearing, pleasant, a little quiet. Wearing thick glasses. HEENT unremarkable, neck supple, no thyroid enlargement. Heart RRR without murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender. No edema. Skin unremarkable where examined. Mood fine, affect appropriate.

PHQ-9 2, GAD-7 3.

A/P
1. Health maintenance, new patient. Baseline CBC, CMP, lipids, TSH. One-time HIV and hep C screening offered and accepted. Pap per old records (she thinks one was done last year). Flu shot next month when stock is in; she has had her COVID primary series per her card.
2. Family history of stroke, noted. Nothing to do at her age with normal BP.
3. Myopia, longstanding. Suggested she get back to an eye doctor this year.

Follow up for a physical in the spring.

documents.title: Office Visit - Psychotic Symptoms
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seen with her sister, who called yesterday.

S: Since roughly October Sharon has been hearing voices commenting on her when no one is around. She believes her former coworkers have been coordinating against her and talking about her. Left her administrative job in late 2022 because of it. Guarded, answers in short phrases, sister fills in. No visual hallucinations reported. Denies thoughts of self-harm or harming others, no plan, no intent. Sleep broken. No alcohol, no cannabis or other drugs, no new medications or supplements. No head injury, headaches, fevers or seizures.

O: Vitals normal, afebrile. Thin, glasses, casually dressed. Alert, oriented to person, place and date. Eye contact limited, affect flat, speech sparse but coherent. Endorses auditory hallucinations; not obviously responding to them in the room. Insight limited, though she is willing to see a specialist. Neuro grossly nonfocal, gait normal. PHQ-9 6.

A/P: New psychotic symptoms over about five months in a 28 year old with a maternal uncle with schizophrenia. Not acutely dangerous today by her and her sister's account, safety plan reviewed, sister staying with her.
- Urgent outpatient psychiatry referral placed, marked expedited. Our referral coordinator to call today.
- Psychiatry to do their own intake labs and tox; she would rather have one blood draw, which is reasonable.
- Crisis line and ED precautions repeated to both of them.
- Check in by phone next week.

50 minutes, most of it history from both and coordinating.

documents.title: Follow-up call
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Spoke with sister and briefly with Sharon. Psychiatry intake is set for 4/12. No change, no safety concerns, sleeping a bit more. Sister knows to call sooner.

medications.sig: Take 1 tablet by mouth at bedtime

documents.title: Outpatient Psychiatry Consultation
documents.author: psychiatry
documents.body:
OUTPATIENT PSYCHIATRY - INITIAL EVALUATION
Visit date: 04/12/2023
Referral source: primary care, expedited

Identifying information: 28 year old married woman, previously employed in office administration, accompanied by her sister.

Presenting problem: For about half a year she has heard voices that others do not hear, and she holds a fixed belief that her coworkers from her last job are conspiring against her. She also reports that her thoughts are being sent out so that other people can hear them.

Psychiatric history: No prior psychiatric treatment, no hospitalizations, no suicide attempts.
Substance use: denies alcohol, cannabis and other drugs. Never smoker.
Family psychiatric history: maternal uncle with schizophrenia; mother with major depressive disorder.
Medical: no chronic conditions. No medications prior to today. No known drug allergies.

Mental status: Alert and oriented x3. Appears anxious. Affect blunted. Thought process mostly linear, slowed. Thought content with persecutory delusions and thought broadcasting. Endorses auditory hallucinations. Denies suicidal and homicidal ideation. Insight partial, judgment fair.
Physical examination: unremarkable.

Studies: CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel and thyroid function within normal limits. Urine toxicology screen negative.

Impression: Schizophrenia. Symptoms present about six months with functional decline, no mood episode, no substance or medical cause found.

Plan:
1. Start risperidone 2 mg by mouth at bedtime.
2. Psychoeducation given to patient and sister.
3. Return in 3 to 4 weeks.
4. We ask primary care to follow weight, glucose and lipids on antipsychotic therapy.

Thank you for this referral.
Outpatient Psychiatry

No eye pain, no red eye, no flashes. Last eye exam was about three years ago. Dad has very bad nearsightedness and had a detached retina.

Meds: risperidone 2 mg qhs (psychiatry).
NKDA.

Exam: vitals and weight in flowsheet. Calm, flat, more conversational than in March. Wearing glasses, conjunctivae clear, pupils equal and reactive. Heart and lungs normal. No tremor, no rigidity on passive movement.

A/P
1. Schizophrenia, on risperidone through psychiatry. Baseline A1c and fasting lipids today for metabolic monitoring as psychiatry asked; weight today is our baseline on the drug.
2. Worsening myopia with a family history of retinal detachment. Referral to ophthalmology. Reviewed sudden floaters, flashes or a curtain over vision as reasons to go in the same day.
3. Physical overdue (missed in January), rebook for later this year.

documents.title: Ophthalmology Consultation
documents.author: ophthalmology
documents.body:
OPHTHALMOLOGY CONSULTATION
Exam date: 06/12/2023
Reason for referral: decreasing distance vision

History: 28 year old woman seen by psychiatry this spring for schizophrenia. Two years of slowly worsening distance vision: street signs are hard to make out and she has trouble telling who someone is from across a room. Has worn glasses since childhood. Her most recent eye exam, three years back, found a correction of -5.50 diopters in each eye. Denies pain, redness and photopsia. Father has high myopia and a history of retinal detachment.
Medications: risperidone 2 mg at bedtime.
Allergies: no known drug allergies.

Examination:
Uncorrected visual acuity 20/200 OD and OS, improving to 20/30 OD and OS with -7.00 D sphere.
Pupils equal, round, reactive, no afferent defect. Intraocular pressures normal. Anterior segment quiet both eyes, lenses clear.
Dilated fundus examination: tessellated fundus both eyes with thin, pale-appearing optic discs consistent with myopic change. Peripheral retina examined 360 degrees: no tears, holes or detachment.

Assessment: Degenerative (pathologic) high myopia, both eyes.

Plan: Updated spectacle prescription provided. Dilated examination yearly. Reviewed symptoms of retinal detachment (new floaters, flashes, a shadow in the vision) and the need to be seen urgently if they occur.

Ophthalmology

GYNECOLOGY - NEW CONSULT
Date of service: 08/17/2023
Referred by primary care for pain with intercourse

HPI: 28 year old who has had pain for six months whenever her partner attempts vaginal penetration. The pain is significant and predictable, and she now avoids sexual activity. No discharge, odor or bleeding. Also recently evaluated by psychiatry (auditory hallucinations) and ophthalmology (progressive myopia).
PMH: schizophrenia; high myopia.
Medications: risperidone 2 mg nightly.
Allergies: NKDA.
Family history: mother with major depressive disorder; father with degenerative myopia; sister without psychiatric illness, her main support; maternal Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry.
Social: never smoker, no alcohol. Not currently employed; previously an administrative assistant.

Vitals: within normal limits.
Abdomen: soft, nontender, no masses.
Pelvic: external genitalia normal in appearance, no lesions, no erythema. Attempted insertion of a small speculum caused severe pain and was stopped; she reports this is the same pain she has with intercourse. Visibly anxious throughout. Bimanual not performed.

Labs: CBC unremarkable; UA unremarkable; vaginal cultures showed no growth.

Assessment: Genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder. No infection or structural lesion identified.

Plan:
- Referral to pelvic floor physical therapy for evaluation and dilator-based therapy.
- Discussed the role of anxiety and the pain cycle; she may benefit from therapy alongside PT.
- Return as needed.

Obstetrics & Gynecology

documents.title: Annual Preventive Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Annual exam. Sister in the waiting room.

Interval: psychiatry switched risperidone to aripiprazole in late September (we learned from the pharmacy). She thinks it is "about the same"; still hears voices most days, less upsetting than in the spring. Sees psychiatry monthly. Ophthalmology: new glasses, letter in chart, degenerative high myopia, yearly dilated exams. Gyn: genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder, went to pelvic PT three times then stopped because of transportation.

She says she gets very keyed up before any medical visit, worse before anything involving a pelvic exam; heart pounding, can't think, wants to leave. Not every day, mostly tied to appointments. GAD-7 9, PHQ-9 5. No SI.

Meds: aripiprazole 15 mg daily (psych). NKDA.
Social: not working. Lives with husband and sister. Never smoker, no alcohol.

Exam: vitals in flowsheet, normal; weight up about 2 kg since May. Anxious but cooperative. Thick lenses. Neck without adenopathy. Heart regular without murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender. Extremities without edema. No abnormal movements.

A/P
1. Health maintenance. Pap is due (last 2020); she declines a speculum exam today and would rather have it done at gyn when she feels ready. Respected. Flu and COVID done in October.
2. Schizophrenia on aripiprazole, psychiatry managing. CBC, CMP, lipids, A1c today.
3. Situational anxiety around medical encounters. Talked through it; she will raise it with psychiatry since they know her meds. We will keep visits predictable and explain exams beforehand.
4. Degenerative high myopia, ophthalmology yearly.
5. Genito-pelvic pain disorder, gyn and PT. Gave her the Medicaid ride number.

RTC 4 months.

documents.title: Psychiatry progress letter
documents.author: psychiatry
documents.body:
To the primary care physician,

This is to update you on our mutual patient. After adequate trials of risperidone (April to September 2023) and aripiprazole (September 2023 to January 2024), she continued to have persistent auditory hallucinations and persecutory ideas. On 01/09/2024 aripiprazole was discontinued and clozapine was started with a standard titration. She reached 300 mg at bedtime on 02/02/2024 and remains on that dose.

Absolute neutrophil counts are being drawn through our clinic's laboratory per the clozapine monitoring schedule, weekly for now; results to date are normal. We will copy you periodically.

We would appreciate continued metabolic monitoring on your end (weight, A1c, lipids). Please let us know of any fever, sore throat or signs of infection you see, as those need an ANC the same day.

Outpatient Psychiatry

documents.author: gynecology
documents.body:
OBSTETRICS & GYNECOLOGY - RETURN VISIT
Date of service: 02/12/2024
Visit type: preconception counseling

She returns, last seen here in August for genito-pelvic pain. She and her husband would like to start a family. Her ancestry is Ashkenazi Jewish and she is worried about inherited disease, above all the chance that a child of hers could be affected by Tay-Sachs; a cousin was diagnosed with it. Her husband, 30, is of mixed European ancestry and knows of no genetic conditions in his family. He attended the visit and asked what comes next.

History: schizophrenia, currently on clozapine; high myopia, degenerative type; genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder evaluated here.
Medications: clozapine 300 mg at bedtime.
Allergies: NKDA.
ROS: no complaints.
Exam: unremarkable.

Genetic testing: carrier testing for Tay-Sachs disease identified a pathogenic HEXA variant. She is a heterozygous carrier.

Counseling: As a carrier she is not expected to have symptoms. A child would be at risk only if her partner is also a carrier; in that case each pregnancy would carry a 1 in 4 chance of an affected child. Carrier screening of her husband is recommended before conception. Options if both are carriers were reviewed in general terms. They will contact our genetics counselor to arrange his testing.

Obstetrics & Gynecology

documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT PHYSICIAN RECORD
Arrival 08/10/2024 16:25

Chief complaint: abdominal pain, severe.

HPI: 29 year old woman with schizophrenia on clozapine. Abdominal pain for two days, steadily worse. Appears anxious. Requested pain medication repeatedly during the visit; after analgesics she continued to rate the pain as severe.

Past history as given by patient: several prior admissions at other hospitals for joint pain, chest pain and on-and-off diarrhea, never with a firm diagnosis despite extensive testing. States she had an exploratory abdominal operation at another hospital but cannot name it or provide records.
Medications: clozapine 300 mg qhs.
Allergies: NKDA.
Social: never smoker, no alcohol, unemployed.

Exam: vitals per nursing flowsheet, unremarkable. Abdomen soft, mild diffuse tenderness without rebound or guarding. A small well-healed lower abdominal scar, which she attributes to the surgery above. Remainder of exam unremarkable.

Results: Hgb 13.2, WBC 7.0, platelets 250. Amylase 45 and lipase 50, both normal. Liver tests within normal limits. Urinalysis normal.

Course: Comparison with outside records obtained during the visit showed inconsistencies between the histories she has given at earlier admissions. Emergency psychiatry was consulted; her presentation was felt to be most consistent with factitious disorder imposed on self. No acute surgical or medical process identified. Findings discussed with the patient in a nonconfrontational way.

Impression: 1. Abdominal pain, no acute cause found. 2. Factitious disorder imposed on self.
Disposition: discharged home with her sister. Follow up with primary care and her psychiatrist.

Emergency Medicine

documents.body:
Physical.

ED record from August arrived 9/16 after a second request. Workup for the abdominal pain negative (Hgb 13.2, WBC 7.0, amylase and lipase normal, LFTs and UA normal). ED and their psychiatry consultant documented factitious disorder imposed on self, noting inconsistencies with outside admissions for joint pain, chest pain and diarrhea; none of those were reported to us at intake and none are in the prior-practice records. She also gave the ED a history of an abdominal operation elsewhere; we have no surgical history on file. I raised the ED's findings with her gently today. She listened, said little, did not want to discuss it further. Psychiatry is aware per the ED record.

Psych: clozapine 300 mg qhs, stable for a few months now by her and her sister's account, fewer voices. Weekly lab visits for ANC at psychiatry, recently spaced out.

Eyes: ophthalmology letter June, stable high myopia, no tears.

Gyn: husband still hasn't had carrier screening. They are holding off on pregnancy for now.

Meds: clozapine 300 mg qhs. NKDA. Never smoker, no alcohol.

Exam: vitals normal, weight 65 kg. Calm, organized, affect restricted. Glasses. Thyroid normal size. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender; small healed lower abdominal scar. No edema.

PHQ-9 3, GAD-7 6.

A/P
1. Health maintenance. Pap overdue; she again prefers to wait. Vaccines done in October.
2. Schizophrenia on clozapine, improving. CMP, lipids, A1c, TSH today.
3. Factitious disorder imposed on self, per ED and emergency psychiatry. Added to problem list. Plan: one primary care physician, consistent follow-up, avoid unnecessary testing, coordinate with psychiatry.
4. Situational anxiety, stable.
5. Tay-Sachs carrier, partner screening pending on their end.
6. Degenerative high myopia, yearly ophthalmology.

RTC 6 months.

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY MEDICINE - PHYSICIAN NOTE
Arrival: 02/06/2025 19:40 by ambulance

CC: seizure at home, witnessed.

HPI: 30 year old woman with schizophrenia. Family saw a generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home this evening; no prior seizure history. Per psychiatry history she has been stable on clozapine for about six months, having not responded to two earlier antipsychotics. Family states she takes it every night as prescribed.
Medications: clozapine 300 mg nightly.
Allergies: NKDA.
Social: never smoker, no alcohol, no drug use.

Vitals on arrival: T 37.2 C (99.0 F), BP 130/85, HR 88, RR 16.
Exam: postictal, becoming more alert over the first hour. Neurological examination nonfocal. No tongue laceration noted. Remainder unremarkable.

Labs: Na 140, K 4.1, Ca 9.2, Mg 2.0. CBC within normal limits. Serum clozapine 650 ng/mL (reference 350-600).

Assessment: Generalized tonic-clonic seizure, attributed to clozapine; level above the usual therapeutic range. Electrolytes normal.
Plan: observed until back to baseline. Discussed with on-call psychiatry, who will review dosing at her outpatient visit. Seizure precautions reviewed with patient and sister. Discharged home. Follow up with primary care this week and with outpatient psychiatry.

Emergency Medicine

documents.body: ED note from 2/6 seizure visit faxed by the hospital at the sister's request. Scanned, flagged for PCP before Wednesday's visit.

documents.title: Sister - ED visit last night
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Sister called. Sharon had a seizure at home last evening, shaking all over for about a minute, then very sleepy. Ambulance to the ED, home around 3 am. Told it was likely from the clozapine and the level was a little high. She is tired but talking normally this morning, no further episodes. No driving (she does not drive anyway). Seizure safety reviewed: no baths alone, no heights, call 911 for a seizure longer than five minutes or a second one. Visit with PCP Wednesday 2/12. Asked sister to bring the discharge papers.

Seen with sister after the ED visit on 2/6 for a first generalized seizure. ED record came on 2/10: nonfocal exam, normal sodium, calcium and magnesium, normal CBC, clozapine level 650 (above their reference range). Attributed to clozapine.

Since then no further events. A bit sore the next day, otherwise back to herself. Psychiatry saw her on Monday: they are keeping clozapine at 300 mg at bedtime. No new medicines.

Exam: vitals normal. Alert, oriented, answering appropriately. Cranial nerves intact, strength and sensation symmetric, reflexes equal, gait steady.

A/P
1. Clozapine-induced seizure. Problem list updated. Dosing is psychiatry's decision; their plan is no change. Seizure precautions reviewed again; she does not drive.
2. Schizophrenia, on clozapine, psychiatry managing.
Return in May as planned, sooner for any further event.

ED VISIT SUMMARY / OBSERVATION DISCHARGE
Arrived 08/15/2025 11:50; discharged from observation 08/16/2025 14:20

Presenting complaint: confusion, lethargy.

History: 30 year old woman with schizophrenia and a prior seizure attributed to clozapine. Taking her antipsychotic as prescribed. The sister she lives with reports that for the last several days she has been drinking very large volumes of water, saying she is always thirsty.
Medications: clozapine 300 mg at bedtime. Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: vital signs stable. Disoriented to time and place. No focal neurologic deficit.

Labs: sodium 125, potassium 4.0, chloride 96, bicarbonate 24, BUN 10. Serum osmolality 260, urine osmolality 80 (maximally dilute).

Assessment: hypotonic hyponatremia from psychogenic polydipsia.
Course: fluid restriction, serial sodium checks, observation overnight. Mental status back to baseline and sodium improving by the next day.
Discharge instructions: fluid restriction as instructed, daily morning weights at home, follow up with primary care within one week and with psychiatry.

Emergency Medicine

documents.author: MA
documents.body: ED and observation summary 8/15 to 8/16 received. Labs abstracted and filed. Routed to PCP.

documents.body: Sister reports Sharon was confused Friday and was taken to the ED; her sodium was low from drinking too much water. Kept overnight, home Saturday afternoon. Told to limit fluids and weigh every morning. More like herself now. Post-ED visit set for Wednesday; sister will request the ED summary be sent to us.

Since home: sister is measuring her water in a marked bottle, she is staying within the limit most days, and doing a morning weight. Thirst still bothers her. Thinking clear. Clozapine 300 mg qhs unchanged.

Exam: vitals normal. Alert and oriented x3. No edema. Mucous membranes moist. Neuro nonfocal.

A/P
1. Psychogenic polydipsia with hyponatremia, per ED. BMP today. Continue the fluid limit and daily weights; a jump of more than a couple of pounds in a day, headache, vomiting or confusion means a same-day call. Psychiatry informed by sister.
2. Schizophrenia on clozapine.
3. Problem list updated.

EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT NOTE
Date of service: 02/09/2026, arrival 15:10

Chief complaint: behavior change.

HPI: 31 year old with established schizophrenia, recent history of a clozapine-associated seizure and of psychogenic polydipsia, brought in by her sister for two days of erratic behavior and talking to herself. According to the sister she has not been taking her medications for about a month.
Medications listed: clozapine 300 mg at bedtime (not taking).
Allergies: NKDA.
Social: unemployed, lives with her sister. No history of substance use.

Vitals: within normal limits.
Exam: disheveled. Appears to be responding to internal stimuli. Agitated; states she has been chosen to defend the world against an alien invasion. No focal neurologic findings.

Labs: Na 140, K 4.1, Cl 102, HCO3 24, BUN 18, Cr 0.9, glucose 98, Ca 9.2. CBC within normal limits. Urine toxicology negative.

Impression: acute exacerbation of schizophrenia in the setting of a month off clozapine. No medical cause found.
Disposition: evaluated by emergency psychiatry; admitted to the inpatient psychiatric unit.

Emergency Medicine

documents.title: Inpatient Psychiatry Discharge Summary
documents.author: psychiatry
documents.body:
INPATIENT PSYCHIATRY - DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 02/10/2026 from the emergency department. Discharged 02/27/2026.

Reason for admission: psychotic relapse of schizophrenia (auditory hallucinations, grandiose and persecutory delusions, agitation) after about one month without clozapine.

Hospital course: Because more than two days had passed since her last dose, clozapine was restarted at a low dose and re-titrated, with ANC monitoring, reaching 300 mg at bedtime before discharge. Agitation settled within the first week. Hallucinations decreased and she became organized and able to engage in planning. Fluid intake was monitored on the unit given her history of psychogenic polydipsia. No seizures during the stay.

Condition at discharge: calm, linear, denies suicidal and homicidal ideation, accepting of medication.

Discharge medication: clozapine 300 mg by mouth at bedtime.
Allergies: NKDA.

Follow-up: outpatient psychiatry within one week; ANC per the monitoring schedule; primary care follow-up. Sister to supervise medication.

Inpatient Psychiatry

She had stopped her clozapine around the new year without telling anyone, became very disorganized, and on Monday the sister took her to the ED; she was admitted from there. Sister apologized for the missed January visit. Asked her to let us know when she is discharged so we can see her. Will request records.

First visit since the February ED visit and inpatient psychiatry stay (2/10 to 2/27 per sister). Neither the ED note nor the discharge summary has reached us despite a request in February; re-requested today.

History from Sharon and her sister: stopped clozapine around the start of the year, "felt fine and didn't think I needed it." Became disorganized; sister took her to the ED 2/9 and she was admitted. Clozapine restarted and slowly increased back to 300 mg at bedtime in the hospital. Since discharge she takes it every night with her sister watching. Seeing psychiatry every two weeks for now, ANC at their lab. Voices quieter. No seizures. Keeping to her fluid limit, no confusion, no swelling.

Meds: clozapine 300 mg qhs. NKDA.

Exam: vitals in flowsheet, normal. Neatly dressed, calm, a little slowed, linear, affect restricted. No tremor. Heart regular. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft. No edema. Neuro nonfocal.

PHQ-9 5, GAD-7 6. No SI.

A/P
1. Schizophrenia, relapse after stopping clozapine, now back on 300 mg qhs with supervised dosing; psychiatry following closely. CBC with diff today since we are drawing.
2. Psychogenic polydipsia: BMP today for sodium.
3. Clozapine-induced seizure: none.
4. Health maintenance: Pap still declined. Vaccines current for the season.
Follow up in about three months, sooner as needed. Sister has our direct line.
